title: A city is not an observation
caption: The same city can have several weather observations.

tables.label: cities
tables.keyDetail: The tutorial does not enforce this; two cities with the same name would break it.
tables.detail: San Francisco has one city row in the tutorial sample.

parts.label: location
parts.detail: A point: two numbers for where the city is.

risks.label: Two cities, one name
risks.detail:
Nothing stops a second San Francisco row.
Every reading would then match both.

work.label: Make name the key
work.detail: The tutorial's next chapter declares name as the primary key.

tables.label: weather
tables.keyDetail: Holds for this sample; two readings on one day would break it.
tables.detail: San Francisco appears on two dates; Hayward appears once.

parts.label: temp_lo, temp_hi
parts.detail: Low and high temperature, whole numbers.

risks.label: A reading with no city
risks.detail: Hayward has a weather row and no city row.

work.label: Point city at cities
work.detail: A foreign key rejects a reading for a city that is not listed.

links.label: name = city
links.detail: The San Francisco city row pairs with two observations, repeating its location.

links.label: city = name
links.detail:
Each reading finds at most one city. Hayward finds none.
Check city names are unique before relying on this.

footnote: Based on the tutorial sample; nothing here checks the real tables.
summary: A weather row is one reading for one city on one day; joining to cities is safe, joining the other way repeats city rows.
